title: The Subjectivity of Monoculture

cost.compute_notes: PDF read directly (pages 1-7) after the summariser's paraphrase proved generic and partly wrong; no artifacts run

triggers: how do I choose a null model for agreement
two models agree more than chance -- than WHICH chance
item difficulty confound in model comparison
why did the correlation disappear when I controlled for difficulty
does my correlation result depend on which models I included

claims.statement: For any joint distribution of binary outcomes across m models there exists a latent variable given which the models are conditionally independent Bernoulli with the observed marginals; consequently a sufficiently expressive null model can always reinterpret cross-model correlation as latent item/model structure.
claims.scope: Theorem 1, with a discrete mixing measure supported on at most 2^m points; de Finetti-style representation. Formal, not empirical.

our_assessment.why: The theorem is correct and its consequence is the single most important fact in this literature: monoculture is not an identifiable property of a dataset, it is a discrepancy from a baseline the analyst chooses and must defend. We demonstrated it accidentally and concretely: a natural nonparametric per-item null we built has algebraically ZERO expected excess on any dataset, which is their asymptotic result appearing exactly at n=1 item.

claims.statement: Adding item difficulty to the null substantially attenuates inferred cross-model correlation relative to nulls that adjust only for model capability; some pairwise correlations flip from strongly positive to slightly negative, while the pairwise ordering remains relatively stable.
claims.scope: HELM (n=14042 items, m=72 models) and HuggingFace Open LLM Leaderboard (n=11994, m=451), binary correctness only; IRT-0.5 (ability only, ~= Kim25/Goel25 implicit null) vs IRT-1 (ability + item difficulty), probit link, L2 penalties.

quantities.name: MIRT_K_sweep
quantities.value: MSE and mean|residual corr| decrease monotonically, log-linear in K

our_assessment.why: Independently corroborated here by a different route: a nonparametric distractor-level null rather than IRT on binary correctness. We find over a third of pairs (35.5%) go negative, which is stronger than their wording ('some even flipping') suggests. Convergent evidence from a different method is worth more than agreement from the same method.

claims.statement: Inferences about excess correlation depend on the population of models and items analysed, and are least identifiable exactly when that population is homogeneous.
claims.scope: Prop 4 (population relativity of the null fit) and Thm 5 (a heterogeneity measure h(I,J) = min eigenvalue of the fitted factor covariances bounds how well the latent representation is identified). Demonstrated on HELM and on ACSIncome with controlled RF/LR/MLP populations.

our_assessment.why: Structurally important and rarely stated: the measurement degrades precisely in the regime the field cares about (a homogeneous ecosystem). It also implies our own numbers are population-relative -- our 22-model sample is a choice, not a view from nowhere.

claims.statement: On the HuggingFace leaderboard, residual model clusters after fitting a 2-D IRT null track contributor/provenance (who fine-tuned or merged the model), not question-type specialisation.
claims.scope: K=2 MIRT on HF; PCA of accuracy stratified by question type as the competing explanation.

quantities.name: PCA_variance_explained_PC1_accuracy_by_question_type
quantities.baseline: if specialisation existed, several PCs would matter

our_assessment.why: Compelling and directly relevant to the twins-vs-co-trained-raters question: what residual structure survives a good null is shared PIPELINE, not shared skill profile. Narrower scope because HF is dominated by community merges/fine-tunes of a few bases, an ecosystem whose provenance structure is unusually strong; HELM (closed models) collapses to ~1 dimension instead. They say so themselves.

checked.how: read arXiv abs page + full PDF pages 1-7 looking for a repository or data-availability statement
checked.result: No code or data link in v1. Ironic given that the paper's whole argument is that the null-model choice must be inspectable: the null-fitting code is precisely what a reader would need to check. Datasets used are public (HELM, HF leaderboard, ACSIncome) so the inputs are recoverable; the IRT fitting is not.
Per-model detail files require accepting repository terms per model, which is why kim2025 could not ship a single tall dataframe for HF. Practical barrier to any reanalysis of the HF half.

relations.why: Does not dispute the measured 0.60; disputes that it licenses an inference about dependence, by showing the baseline it is measured against is a free choice.
relations.asymmetric_note: Not cito:refutes. The reciprocal edge on kim2025 is NOT 'refuted-by' -- the number stands, the interpretation does not. Recording this as refutation would be the commonest way this pair gets miscited later.

relations.why: Explicitly names Kim et al.'s implicit null as one that 'does not incorporate item-level heterogeneity'.
Nikhil Garg on both. Weight this as self-correction.
Reuses the same HELM and HF response matrices.
We tested c1 and c2 by a distractor-level route they explicitly set aside (they work on binary correctness only).

Reciprocal. Jo et al.'s Theorem 1 (a rich enough null absorbs any monoculture discrepancy) has a structural twin in a literature that never cites it: a code re-execution RATE is a discrepancy from a denominator the analyst chooses, and Trisovic et al.'s exclusion rule absorbs half the failures (39.8% vs 19.3% on identical logs). Both papers take the reference class as given.

Reciprocal, and the more instructive of the two instances of this edge. A reproducibility rate is a proportion whose denominator is chosen partway down a funnel, exactly as a monoculture statistic is a discrepancy from a chosen null. Samuel & Mietchen PRINT the whole ladder, which protects the headline -- and their decay analysis is still not identifiable, because it is computed on the conditioned subset. Printing the null is not the same as choosing it.

open_questions: They state their null uses binary correctness and that answer-choice identity 'indeed provides additional information about cross-model agreement'. That gap is exactly where we found the ability-graded concentration effect. Does a nominal-response IRT model (Bock 1972), which models attraction to each distractor, close it?

If monoculture is only defined relative to a defended null, what null should a REGULATOR use? The paper reframes the problem elegantly and leaves the normative question open, and that question is the reason anyone measures this.

Their heterogeneity measure h(I,J) suggests a practical protocol: deliberately include maximally diverse models/items to make the null identifiable. Nobody has operationalised that as a benchmark-design rule.
